--- title: "Greek Public Debt: How Much, to Whom, and Can Greece Repay It?" author: "" output: html_document: css: styles.css theme: flatly highlight: tango toc: true toc_float: true code_folding: show self_contained: true vignette: > %\VignetteIndexEntry{Greek Public Debt} %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown} %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8} --- ## What is this? Greece went through one of the deepest debt crises of any modern European economy. More than fifteen years after the first bailout, this story answers four questions with official data: 1. **Does Greece owe more now than in 2010?** 2. **Whom does it owe?** 3. **How much is that compared with the size of the economy, and with the rest of the EU?** 4. **Will Greece be able to repay?** The data come from three places: - **Eurostat**, the statistical office of the EU: the debt, the deficit, the interest, who holds the debt and when it falls due. They are downloaded when the page is rendered, so a new render brings in the latest figures. - **The World Bank**: interest payments as a share of the government's revenue, back to 1972. - **The Public Debt Management Agency (PDMA)** of Greece: who the creditors are, from its *Annual Debt Bulletin 2025*. The bulletin is a PDF, so its figures are typed in below, with the page they come from. It follows two other stories of this site: [Greece Since 2000](ILLUSTRATION_GREECE_SINCE_2000.Rmd) goes through the boom, the crisis and the recovery of the economy, and [Same Crisis, Different Endings](ILLUSTRATION_EURO_CRISIS.Rmd) compares Greece with the other countries of the euro crisis; this one follows the debt. **Two measures of the same debt.** Eurostat and the EU count the debt of the whole *general government* (the State, public bodies, local government and the pension funds) and leave out what one public body owes another: that is the figure of the EU rules, and of the headlines. The PDMA also reports the debt of *the State* alone, which includes the short-term loans that other public bodies make to the State with their spare cash. At the end of 2025 the first was **€362.9 billion**, the second **€406.2 billion**. This story uses the first, except where it names the creditors of the State. --- ## Packages ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # install.packages(c("eurostat", "plotly", "jsonlite")) library(eurostat) library(plotly) ``` ::: ## The data ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # a Eurostat dataset, without its missing values eurostat_values <- function(id, filters) { x <- get_eurostat(id, filters = filters, time_format = "num", cache = FALSE) as.data.frame(x[!is.na(x$values), ]) } # debt, deficit and interest of the general government of Greece edp <- eurostat_values("gov_10dd_edpt1", list( geo = "EL", sector = "S13", na_item = c("GD", "GD_F3", "GD_F4", "B9", "D41PAY"), unit = c("MIO_EUR", "PC_GDP") )) # gross domestic product at current prices, million euros gdp <- eurostat_values("nama_10_gdp", list(geo = "EL", na_item = "B1GQ", unit = "CP_MEUR")) # one series of the deficit and debt data, by year series <- function(item, unit, years) { s <- edp[edp$na_item == item & edp$unit == unit, ] s$values[match(years, s$time)] } years <- sort(unique(edp$time[edp$na_item == "GD"])) greece <- data.frame( year = years, debt_bn = series("GD", "MIO_EUR", years) / 1000, # debt, billion euros debt_gdp = series("GD", "PC_GDP", years), # debt, % of GDP bonds_bn = series("GD_F3", "MIO_EUR", years) / 1000, # of which bonds and bills loans_bn = series("GD_F4", "MIO_EUR", years) / 1000, # of which loans balance_gdp = series("B9", "PC_GDP", years), # surplus (+) or deficit (-), % of GDP interest_gdp = series("D41PAY", "PC_GDP", years), # interest, % of GDP interest_bn = series("D41PAY", "MIO_EUR", years) / 1000, gdp_bn = gdp$values[match(years, gdp$time)] / 1000 ) # the balance before interest: what the State collects minus what it spends on everything else greece$primary_gdp <- greece$balance_gdp + greece$interest_gdp last <- max(greece$year) at <- function(column, year) greece[[column]][greece$year == year] # who holds the debt (from 2020), and when it falls due holders <- eurostat_values("gov_10dd_ggd", list(geo = "EL", sector = "S13", na_item = "GD", maturity = "TOTAL", unit = "MIO_EUR")) due <- eurostat_values("gov_10dd_rmd", list(geo = "EL", sector = "S13", na_item = "GD")) # debt of every EU country, % of GDP, and the countries with the most eu <- eurostat_values("gov_10dd_edpt1", list(sector = "S13", na_item = "GD", unit = "PC_GDP")) eu_name <- c(setNames(eu_countries$name, eu_countries$code), EU27_2020 = "EU-27") most <- eu[eu$time == last & eu$geo %in% eu_countries$code, ] most <- most[order(-most$values), ] # the average years to repayment of the debt of every EU country, the longest first maturities <- eurostat_values("gov_10dd_rmd", list(sector = "S13", na_item = "GD", maturity = "TOTAL", unit = "YR")) maturities <- maturities[maturities$time == max(maturities$time) & maturities$geo %in% eu_countries$code, ] maturities <- maturities[order(-maturities$values), ] # World Bank: interest payments, % of revenue world_bank <- jsonlite::fromJSON("https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/GRC/indicator/GC.XPN.INTP.RV.ZS?format=json&per_page=100")[[2]] interest_revenue <- data.frame(year = as.integer(world_bank$date), value = world_bank$value) interest_revenue <- interest_revenue[!is.na(interest_revenue$value), ] interest_revenue <- interest_revenue[order(interest_revenue$year), ] ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} greek_red <- "#d62728" gray <- "#9e9e9e" blue <- "#1f77b4" # the source of a chart, as a note under it, and the common layout chart <- function(p, title, source, y_title = "", annotations = list(), margin = list(t = 70, b = 90), note_y = -0.16, ...) { note <- list( text = paste("Source:", source), xref = "paper", yref = "paper", x = 0, y = note_y, xanchor = "left", yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE, font = list(size = 11, color = gray) ) layout(p, title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left"), yaxis = list(title = y_title), xaxis = list(title = ""), margin = margin, annotations = c(annotations, list(note)), ... ) %>% config(displaylogo = FALSE) } # a short label of an amount billion <- function(x) paste0("€", format(round(x), big.mark = ","), " bn") ``` ::: --- ## 1. Does Greece owe more now than in 2010? **In euros, yes. As a share of the economy, slightly less — and far less than at the peak.** At the end of 2010 the Greek state owed €331 bn; at the end of 2025 it owed €363 bn, that is €32 bn more. The debt fell only once, in 2012, when private holders of Greek bonds took a loss in the restructuring known as the PSI: between 2011 and 2012 the debt went down by €51 bn, although new bailout loans came in at the same time. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} highlight <- ifelse(greece$year %in% c(2010, last), greek_red, gray) plot_ly(greece, x = ~year, y = ~debt_bn, type = "bar", marker = list(color = highlight), hovertemplate = "%{x}: €%{y:.1f} billion" ) %>% chart( "Greek government debt, billion euros", "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1", "Billion euros", annotations = list(list( x = 2012, y = at("debt_bn", 2012), text = "2012: bondholders' haircut (PSI)", showarrow = TRUE, ax = 0, ay = -60 )) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: What matters for paying a debt is the size of the economy that carries it. As a share of the gross domestic product (GDP), the debt was **147.8%** in 2010 and **145.4%** in 2025: about the same. In between it rose to 209.4% in 2020, when the pandemic made the economy shrink, and it has fallen by 64 points since. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_ly(greece, x = ~year, y = ~debt_gdp, type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers", line = list(color = greek_red, width = 3), marker = list(color = greek_red), hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of GDP" ) %>% add_lines(x = range(greece$year), y = c(60, 60), line = list(color = gray, dash = "dash"), hoverinfo = "skip", inherit = FALSE) %>% chart( "Greek government debt, % of GDP", "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1", "% of GDP", showlegend = FALSE, annotations = list( list(x = greece$year[1], y = 60, text = "60%: the limit of the EU rules", showarrow = FALSE, xanchor = "left", yanchor = "bottom", font = list(color = gray)), list(x = greece$year[which.max(greece$debt_gdp)], y = max(greece$debt_gdp), text = "Pandemic", showarrow = TRUE, ax = -50, ay = -30) ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: --- ## 2. Whom does Greece owe? **Mostly the rest of the euro area, through the rescue funds of the bailouts.** In 2010, 79% of the debt was bonds sold to investors; in 2025, 71% is loans. The bailouts replaced most of the bonds with long, cheap loans from the euro area and, until 2022, the IMF. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_ly(greece, x = ~year, y = ~bonds_bn, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Bonds and bills", line = list(color = gray, width = 3), hovertemplate = "%{x}: €%{y:.1f} billion in bonds" ) %>% add_trace(y = ~loans_bn, name = "Loans", line = list(color = greek_red, width = 3), hovertemplate = "%{x}: €%{y:.1f} billion in loans") %>% chart("From bonds to loans: the debt by instrument, billion euros", "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1", "Billion euros", legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The PDMA names the creditors of the State. At the end of 2025: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # PDMA, Annual Debt Bulletin 2025 (June 2026), debt of the State at 31.12.2025, million euros (pages 13-14). # The bulletin gives 211,421 for the loans of the EFSF, the ESM and the GLF together, and says # that the EFSF and the ESM hold 45.58% of the debt; the GLF is the difference. total <- 406181 creditors <- data.frame( creditor = c( "EFSF and ESM: the euro area rescue funds", "Bonds held by investors and the Bank of Greece", "Repos: short-term loans, mostly from public bodies", "GLF: bilateral loans of euro area countries", "Other EU and international loans (RRF, SURE, EIB)", "Treasury bills" ), million = c(round(0.4558 * total), 100759, 62852, 211421 - round(0.4558 * total), 23057, 7969) ) creditors$share <- 100 * creditors$million / total creditors <- creditors[order(creditors$million), ] creditors$creditor <- factor(creditors$creditor, levels = creditors$creditor) plot_ly(creditors, x = ~ million / 1000, y = ~creditor, type = "bar", orientation = "h", marker = list(color = c(rep(gray, nrow(creditors) - 1), greek_red)), text = ~ paste0(round(share, 1), "%"), textposition = "outside", cliponaxis = FALSE, hovertemplate = "%{y}: €%{x:.1f} billion" ) %>% chart("Who lends to the Greek State, end of 2025, billion euros", "PDMA, Annual Debt Bulletin 2025; the GLF as calculated in the code above", margin = list(l = 330, r = 60, t = 70, b = 90)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: - The **EFSF and the ESM**, the rescue funds of the euro area, hold almost half of the debt of the State. Their loans are repaid over decades: those of the EFSF from 2023 to 2070, those of the ESM from 2034 to 2060 (ESM). - The **GLF** loans of the first bailout come from the other euro area countries. Their interest rate floats, so Greece is paying them back early: €5.3 billion in 2025. - The **IMF** was repaid in full in 2022. - The **repos** are mostly the cash of other public bodies, lent to the State for a few days or weeks; the EU measure of the debt leaves them out. Eurostat's view of the same debt, by who holds it rather than by instrument: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} groups <- c( S2 = "Abroad (the rescue funds, foreign investors)", S121 = "Bank of Greece", S122_S123 = "Greek banks", `S124-S129` = "Other Greek financial companies", S11 = "Greek companies", S14_S15 = "Greek households" ) latest_holders <- holders[holders$time == max(holders$time), ] held <- data.frame(holder = groups, million = latest_holders$values[match(names(groups), latest_holders$sector2)]) held$million[is.na(held$million)] <- 0 held$share <- 100 * held$million / latest_holders$values[latest_holders$sector2 == "S1_S2"] held <- held[order(held$share), ] held$holder <- factor(held$holder, levels = held$holder) plot_ly(held, x = ~share, y = ~holder, type = "bar", orientation = "h", marker = list(color = ifelse(held$holder == groups[["S2"]], greek_red, gray)), text = ~ paste0(round(share), "%"), textposition = "outside", cliponaxis = FALSE, hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:.1f}% of the debt" ) %>% chart(paste0("Who holds the Greek government debt, ", max(holders$time), ", % of the debt"), "Eurostat, gov_10dd_ggd", margin = list(l = 300, t = 70, b = 90)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: --- ## 3. How much is it, compared with the economy and with the EU? At **145.4% of GDP**, Greece still has the highest debt in the EU, 8.7 points above Italy. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} eu_latest <- eu[eu$time == last & eu$geo %in% c(eu_countries$code, "EU27_2020"), ] eu_latest$name <- eu_name[eu_latest$geo] eu_latest <- eu_latest[order(eu_latest$values), ] eu_latest$name <- factor(eu_latest$name, levels = eu_latest$name) plot_ly(eu_latest, x = ~values, y = ~name, type = "bar", orientation = "h", marker = list(color = ifelse(eu_latest$geo == "EL", greek_red, ifelse(eu_latest$geo == "EU27_2020", blue, gray))), hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:.1f}% of GDP" ) %>% chart(paste0("Government debt in the EU, ", last, ", % of GDP"), "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1", margin = list(l = 130, t = 70, b = 90)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: --- ## 4. Will Greece be able to repay? Countries rarely pay their debt off; they repay old loans with new ones. The question is whether the debt stays **affordable** — whether the interest leaves enough for everything else — and whether it keeps **shrinking against the economy**. On both, the numbers now look good, for four reasons. ### Interest takes far less of the budget In 2011 interest cost Greece 7.7% of GDP; in 2025, 3.1%. The World Bank's series shows the same from the side of the budget: interest took 17.8% of the government's revenue in 2011, and 7.5% in 2024. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} subplot( plot_ly(greece, x = ~year, y = ~interest_gdp, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", line = list(color = greek_red, width = 3), name = "% of GDP (Eurostat)", hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of GDP"), plot_ly(interest_revenue, x = ~year, y = ~value, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", line = list(color = blue, width = 3), name = "% of revenue (World Bank)", hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of revenue"), nrows = 2, shareX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE ) %>% chart("Interest paid by the Greek government", "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1; World Bank, GC.XPN.INTP.RV.ZS", "% of GDP", yaxis2 = list(title = "% of revenue"), legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ### The debt is long, fixed and in euros ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} years_left <- due[due$unit == "YR" & due$maturity == "TOTAL", ] buckets <- c(Y_LE1 = "Up to 1 year", `Y1-5` = "1 to 5 years", `Y5-10` = "5 to 10 years", `Y10-30` = "10 to 30 years", Y_GT30 = "Over 30 years") falling_due <- due[due$unit == "MIO_EUR" & due$time == max(due$time) & due$maturity %in% names(buckets), ] falling_due$label <- factor(buckets[falling_due$maturity], levels = buckets) falling_due$share <- 100 * falling_due$values / sum(falling_due$values) plot_ly(falling_due, x = ~label, y = ~share, type = "bar", marker = list(color = greek_red), text = ~ paste0(round(share), "%"), textposition = "outside", cliponaxis = FALSE, hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of the debt" ) %>% chart(paste0("When the debt falls due, ", max(due$time), ", % of the debt"), "Eurostat, gov_10dd_rmd", "% of the debt") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: - On average the debt falls due in **18.4 years** (Eurostat), the longest in the EU: next comes Austria, with 11.3 years. - After interest rate swaps, **none of it has a floating rate** and **none is in a foreign currency** (PDMA): higher interest rates reach only the debt that is renewed, a little each year. - In 2025 the State needed **€17.6 billion** to repay maturing debt and cover its budget, about 7% of GDP, and borrowed it at **2.89%** for **14.6 years** on average (PDMA). When the euro area eased the terms of its loans in 2018, it set out to keep these needs below 15% of GDP in the medium term and below 20% after that (Eurogroup, June 2018). - The State keeps a cash reserve: the general government held **€39.6 billion** in cash at the end of 2025, so its debt *minus its cash* was **€323 billion** (PDMA). ### Why the ratio fell so fast The change of the debt ratio each year adds up from four parts: - **Interest** adds to the debt. - **The primary balance** (the budget before interest) adds a deficit or takes away a surplus. - **Growth** of the economy in euros — real growth plus inflation — shrinks the ratio, as the same debt is divided by a bigger GDP. - **Other** changes: debt that changes without a deficit, such as the PSI haircut of 2012 or the cash the State borrows ahead and keeps. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} d <- greece[greece$year >= 2010 & !is.na(greece$gdp_bn), ] n <- nrow(d) ratio <- 100 * d$debt_bn / d$gdp_bn growth <- d$gdp_bn[-1] / d$gdp_bn[-n] - 1 parts <- data.frame( year = d$year[-1], change = diff(ratio), interest = 100 * d$interest_bn[-1] / d$gdp_bn[-1], primary = -d$primary_gdp[-1], growth = -ratio[-n] * growth / (1 + growth) ) parts$other <- parts$change - parts$interest - parts$primary - parts$growth plot_ly(parts, x = ~year, y = ~interest, type = "bar", name = "Interest", marker = list(color = greek_red)) %>% add_trace(y = ~primary, name = "Primary deficit (+) or surplus (-)", marker = list(color = "#ff9896")) %>% add_trace(y = ~growth, name = "Growth of GDP in euros", marker = list(color = blue)) %>% add_trace(y = ~other, name = "Other", marker = list(color = gray)) %>% add_trace(y = ~change, type = "scatter", mode = "markers", name = "Change of the debt ratio", marker = list(color = "black", size = 10, symbol = "diamond")) %>% chart("What changed the debt ratio each year, points of GDP", "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1 and nama_10_gdp; own calculation", "Points of GDP", barmode = "relative", note_y = -0.34, margin = list(t = 70, b = 160), # under the chart, as its five entries take two lines legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = -0.1, yanchor = "top")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: From 2021 the economy grew fast in euros — partly real growth, partly inflation — while the interest rate on the debt stayed low: growth alone took 71 points off the ratio between 2021 and 2025. The budget before interest was in deficit in the pandemic and then turned to surplus: from 2023, the surpluses took 12 points more. ### Where it could go: three scenarios The debt ratio of next year is this year's, grown by the interest rate and shrunk by the growth of GDP in euros, minus the primary surplus: $$d_{t} = d_{t-1} \times \frac{1 + i_t}{1 + g_t} - pb_t$$ The scenarios below start from the 2025 debt and its average interest rate of 2.1%, which climbs over ten years as cheap loans are replaced by new borrowing at market rates. **They are illustrations of what drives the debt, not forecasts.** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} start_rate <- at("interest_bn", last) / at("debt_bn", last - 1) assumptions <- data.frame( scenario = c("Strong", "Steady", "Weak"), growth = c(0.050, 0.040, 0.025), # growth of GDP in euros, a year rate_to = c(0.025, 0.030, 0.040), # average interest rate on the debt after ten years primary = c(3.5, 2.5, 1.0) # primary surplus, % of GDP ) project <- function(growth, rate_to, primary, years = (last + 1):2040) { debt <- at("debt_gdp", last) path <- numeric(length(years)) for (k in seq_along(years)) { rate <- start_rate + (rate_to - start_rate) * min(1, k / 10) debt <- debt * (1 + rate) / (1 + growth) - primary path[k] <- debt } data.frame(year = c(last, years), debt_gdp = c(at("debt_gdp", last), path)) } paths <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(assumptions)), function(k) { cbind(scenario = assumptions$scenario[k], project(assumptions$growth[k], assumptions$rate_to[k], assumptions$primary[k])) })) in_2040 <- setNames(paths$debt_gdp[paths$year == 2040], paths$scenario[paths$year == 2040]) knitr::kable(transform(assumptions, growth = paste0(100 * growth, "%"), rate_to = paste0(100 * rate_to, "%"), primary = paste0(primary, "% of GDP"), debt_2040 = paste0(round(in_2040[scenario]), "% of GDP") ), col.names = c("Scenario", "GDP growth in euros, a year", "Interest rate after ten years", "Primary surplus", "Debt in 2040")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |Scenario |GDP growth in euros, a year |Interest rate after ten years |Primary surplus |Debt in 2040 | |:--------|:---------------------------|:-----------------------------|:---------------|:------------| |Strong |5% |2.5% |3.5% of GDP |55% of GDP | |Steady |4% |3% |2.5% of GDP |86% of GDP | |Weak |2.5% |4% |1% of GDP |150% of GDP | ::: ```{.r .cell-code} plot_ly(greece, x = ~year, y = ~debt_gdp, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Actual", line = list(color = "black", width = 3), hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of GDP" ) %>% add_trace(data = paths[paths$scenario == "Strong", ], name = "Strong", line = list(color = blue, dash = "dot")) %>% add_trace(data = paths[paths$scenario == "Steady", ], name = "Steady", line = list(color = greek_red, dash = "dot")) %>% add_trace(data = paths[paths$scenario == "Weak", ], name = "Weak", line = list(color = gray, dash = "dot")) %>% chart("Greek government debt to 2040: three scenarios, % of GDP", "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1; own scenarios", "% of GDP", legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: In the steady scenario the debt falls to about **86% of GDP by 2040**. In the weak one it ends near 150%, a little above today's level: with long, fixed and cheap loans, a bad decade would stop the fall rather than send the debt back to the heights of 2020. ### So, will Greece repay? On today's numbers, **yes**: the debt is large, but it is cheap, it falls due slowly, and it is shrinking against the economy. The markets agree: Greece is back in the investment grade (Moody's raised it to Baa3 in March 2025), and at the end of 2025 its ten-year bonds paid only 0.59 percentage points more than Germany's (PDMA). What could still go wrong: - **A recession**, or years of slow growth: growth did most of the work since 2021. - **Higher interest rates** on the debt that is renewed each year, and more of it once the cheap rescue loans start falling due in the 2030s. - **Smaller surpluses**: the scenarios need primary surpluses for many years, which is a political choice, not only an economic one. - **An ageing population**, which raises the cost of pensions and health care. --- ## Sources - Eurostat: [gov_10dd_edpt1](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/gov_10dd_edpt1/default/table?lang=en) (deficit, debt and interest), [gov_10dd_ggd](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/gov_10dd_ggd/default/table?lang=en) (holders of the debt), [gov_10dd_rmd](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/gov_10dd_rmd/default/table?lang=en) (remaining maturity), [nama_10_gdp](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/nama_10_gdp/default/table?lang=en) (GDP). - World Bank: [Interest payments (% of revenue), GC.XPN.INTP.RV.ZS](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/GC.XPN.INTP.RV.ZS?locations=GR). - PDMA, Ministry of Finance: [Annual Debt Bulletin 2025](https://minfin.gov.gr/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Annual_Debt_Bulletin_2025GR.pdf) (in Greek, June 2026). - ESM: [When will Greece repay ESM and EFSF loans?](https://www.esm.europa.eu/content/when-will-greece-repay-esm-and-efsf-loans)
